citation: Shamse Tasnim Cynthia, Joy Krishan Das, Banani Roy (University of Saskatchewan). 'Are We All Using Agents the Same Way? An Empirical Study of Core and Peripheral Developers' Use of Coding Agents'. MSR '26 (23rd International Conference on Mining Software Repositories), 13-14 April 2026, Rio de Janeiro. DOI 10.1145/3793302.3793377. Preprint arXiv:2601.20106v1 (27 Jan 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20106. Note: the MSR programme page titles it 'Are We All Using Agents Now?'; the paper itself says 'the Same Way?'.
source_tier: Peer-reviewed (MSR 2026 technical track); read via the arXiv preprint v1, which may differ from the camera-ready ACM version.
access_status: Fully read (full PDF text of arXiv v1 extracted and read for abstract, method, RQ results, threats, acknowledgements). Conference page read for metadata. ACM version not opened.
sponsor_and_incentive: Acknowledgment: NSERC Discovery Grants, Canada Foundation for Innovation John R. Evans Leaders Fund, and industry-stream NSERC CREATE in Software Analytics Research (SOAR). No vendor selling an agent product is named as funder.
exact_quotes: 'In this paper, we present the first empirical study of 9,427 agentic PRs, examining how core and peripheral developers use, review, modify, and verify agent-generated contributions prior to acceptance.' (Abstract)
'We find that, on average, 74.1% of agentic PRs are accepted without modification across both groups.' (Section 1, RQ3)

'In most cases, the agent's contribution was accepted without modification with an average of 74.1% across both developer groups. However, core developers modified a larger share of agentic PRs, representing 28.3% of their 1,060 accepted PRs, compared to 23.5% of the 5,759 PRs accepted by peripheral developers.' (Section 3.3)
'peripheral developers are nearly twice as likely to merge without running any checks on the agentic PR (19.1% vs. 11.2%).' (Section 3.4)
'core developers achieve a higher proportion of "success" outcomes in all the check_suites ... with rates of 51.2% and 43.1%, respectively.' (Section 3.4)
'The median number of comments per agentic PR is higher for core developers (3.6) compared to peripheral developers (2.0).' (Section 3.2)

'Developers may modify agent-generated code through force pushes, which overwrite commit history. Because these edits leave no observable record, some developer interventions may not be captured in our analysis.' (Threats to Validity)
'some PRs may be merged even when checks fail, for example, if test failures are unrelated to the submitted changes.' (Threats to Validity)
'Although trust is inherently subjective, prior studies suggest that it can be inferred from an individual's usage of a system and the nature of tasks they are willing to delegate.' (Section 1, RQ1)
date_and_recency: Preprint 27 Jan 2026; presented 13 April 2026. Data collection cut-off 1 August 2025; agents' PRs from 2025 (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex), so tool versions are mid-2025.
key_claims: First empirical study of core vs peripheral developers using coding agents. (1) Usage rates similar, but a subset of peripheral developers generates disproportionately many agentic PRs; peripheral spread tasks evenly (bug fix, feature, docs, tests), core lean to docs and tests (42.7% combined). (2) Core developers engage slightly more in review discussion; both groups mostly raise evolvability issues. (3) 74.1% of accepted agentic PRs are accepted without modification; when modified, both groups commonly refactor. (4) Peripheral developers more often merge without running CI checks; core developers more consistently require passing checks. Authors also say core PRs reach main/master at a substantially higher rate.
headline_figures: 9,427 closed/resolved agentic PRs, 1,391 repositories, 1,701 developers (390 core, 1,311 peripheral); 6,819 merged (accepted). Unit: PR, GitHub, repos with >=100 stars, data to 1 Aug 2025.

74.1% of accepted PRs accepted without modification (average across the two groups; basis is the 6,819 accepted PRs, not all 9,427). Core: 28.3% of 1,060 accepted PRs modified (about 71.7% unmodified). Peripheral: 23.5% of 5,759 accepted modified (about 76.5% unmodified).

CI (Table 7): average check runs per PR core 9.3, peripheral 8.1; all-success rollup core 51.2% vs peripheral 43.1%; failure core 16.5% vs peripheral 20.0%; no check run core 11.2% vs peripheral 19.1%.

Review: only 1,501 of 6,819 accepted PRs had review comments (9,403 comments). Median comments per agentic PR core 3.6 vs peripheral 2.0 (Mann-Whitney p<0.001, Cliff's delta 0.28, small). Coded sample 340 of 2,735 comments: evolvability about 52.8% (core) and 59.3% (peripheral) [which figure belongs to which group not re-verified from table].
Modification size: core mean added-lines share 55.4% vs 40.4% peripheral; deleted 38.2% vs 24.5%; difference not statistically significant.
Core/peripheral cut: 80th percentile of a PR-based experience score (authored plus reviewed closed PRs / total closed PRs, per repository).
sample_unit_and_population: Pull requests (9,427 closed) on public open-source GitHub repos with >=100 stars, attributed to Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex via search queries (branch prefix or Co-Authored-By trailer). Started from 28,769 PRs / 2,856 developers; filtered to developers with PRs before Jan 2025 and active in only one repo with agentic PRs. 6,819 accepted PRs used for RQ1-RQ4 detail. No enterprise data.
observed_vs_stated: Observed behaviour: mined PR, review comment, commit and CI check-run data. No survey or interviews (listed as future work). Trust is inferred from usage and delegation, which the paper itself concedes is a proxy. PR purpose labels were produced by GPT-4 with human validation on 364 PRs (kappa 80.3%).
what_makes_trust_justified: Paper's position: human review plus automated CI gate before merge ('all checks must pass'). Core developers more consistently require passing CI; authors recommend review rubrics/checklists and AI literacy and governance. Authors note acceptance without modification concentrates in routine tasks (docs, testing).
what_it_costs: Core developers spend more review effort (median 3.6 vs 2.0 comments) and modify more (28.3% vs 23.5%), with larger edits in a subset. Peripheral developers skip this and merge faster. Paper gives no time or delay measurements.
failure_mode_class: Over-reliance / unverified merge (accepting without modification or with CI failing or absent); wrong code that fails project checks (e.g. formatting failures, agent claiming tests pass while CI failed).
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an incident study. Case examples: a peripheral contributor merged a Copilot PR with two integration checks still failing; enforcing required passing checks (branch protection) would have blocked it. Agent reported 'all tests are now passing' while CI still failed.
limitations_stated: Only four agents; GitHub only; >=100 stars bias to popular projects; only developers active after agent introduction and in one repo; single-repo experience metric may misclassify a few; force pushes erase edit history so interventions may be missed; commit-attribution heuristics; CI 'conclusion' field may misrepresent (merged despite unrelated failures); manual coding subjectivity; GPT-4 labelling errors; rejected PRs not studied.
counter_evidence: 74.1% unmodified does not show review was thorough: it is also consistent with rubber-stamping, and only 22% of accepted PRs (1,501/6,819) had any review comments. Unmodified share is for accepted PRs only (rejected PRs excluded), so it is conditioned on acceptance and survivorship-biased. Non-trivial share of PRs have no checks (11 to 19%) or failing checks. Many agentic PRs may be self-merged by the person who prompted the agent, so 'review' may be self-review. No quality outcomes (defects after merge) measured.
verification_status: Checked against the full paper text I opened: 9,427 PRs, 74.1%, 28.3%/23.5%, CI figures 51.2/43.1, 19.1/11.2, medians 3.6/2.0, limitations, funding. Not checked: ACM camera-ready differences; replication package; per-group evolvability percentages in Figure 5 [uncertain].
usable_claim: In a study of 9,427 closed agent-authored pull requests across 1,391 open-source GitHub repos (data to August 2025), the authors report that on average 74.1% of the accepted ones were merged without any modification, and that developers outside a project's core were nearly twice as likely as core developers to merge with no CI checks run (19.1% vs 11.2%). This is observed PR behaviour, not self-report.
do_not_use: Do not say 74.1% of all 9,427 PRs were accepted unmodified (basis is 6,819 accepted PRs, and it is an average of two group rates). Do not read it as proof of good code or of careful review. Do not say 'peripheral developers' means junior or novice (it means low share of PR activity in that repo). Do not claim the study shows trust is justified or measured defects. Do not state evolvability percentages by group without rechecking Figure 5. Do not use the programme-page abstract's 'about three-quarters' as a quote of the paper.
overlap_with_existing_essays: Not checked against the Verification Gap or Checking Isn't Catching essays in this task; caller should grep the essays for 'MSR', '9,427', '74.1' and 'Cynthia' before use. [uncertain]
